blind_target.authors: Lively, S. E., Logan, J. S., & Pisoni, D. B.
blind_target.title: Training Japanese listeners to identify English /r/ and /l/. II: The role of phonetic environment and talker variability in learning new perceptual categories
blind_target.evidence_quote: The goal of the current paper is to replicate the key experiments from Logan et al. (1991) and Lively et al. (1993) and test the hypothesis that using high variability input (specifically, input with multiple talkers) leads to more generalisation in phonetic learning than when low variability input is used.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The current study attempted to replicate the findings of seminal work by Logan and colleagues (1991) and Lively and colleagues (1993), which found that phonetic training with multiple talkers led to greater generalization to novel talkers than single talker training. Across two different measures, our study found no evidence of such effect in a sample of 166 participants. Bayes Factor analyses found that in each case the evidence for a variability benefit was ambiguous.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Central multiple-talker advantage was not supported; ambiguous Bayes factors do not establish the null. Positive general phonetic learning is ancillary to the central contrast.

prior_decision.quote: The goal of the current paper is to replicate the key experiments from Logan et al. (1991) and Lively et al. (1993) and test the hypothesis that using high variability input (specifically, input with multiple talkers) leads to more generalisation in phonetic learning than when low variability input is used.
prior_decision.reason: The paper explicitly re-tests both Logan et al. (1991) and Lively et al. (1993) (specifically Experiment 2 of Lively et al., 1993, providing the single-talker low-variability comparison and the familiar-versus-novel post-test contrast). As settled for the paired Logan et al. (1991) row, the replication outcome for Lively et al. (1993) is 'failed' rather than 'uninformative': the study was high-powered (N = 166, 99% power for the original effect size), found no evidence of the claimed multi-talker generalization advantage across both primary measures, and concluded that any true effect is much smaller than reported in the seminal studies, with the ambiguous Bayes factors reflecting cautious Bayesian interpretation rather than a methodological failure preventing adjudication.

luna_triage.reason: The source explicitly states that its large-sample experiment retests the variability findings from Lively et al. (1993), and its Discussion compares the multiple-talker benefit against the single-talker condition. The cited 1993 paper is an independent original from shipped Logan et al. (1991); the source names and describes both separately.
luna_triage.location: Introduction, paragraph 2; Methods/Results; Discussion, lines 164 and 178; References
luna_triage.omission_quote: In a follow up study, the authors examine the effect of different types of variability in the input stimuli (Lively et al., 1993). They report that participants' ability to generalise to novel stimuli produced by a new talker was specifically dependent on exposure to training stimuli spoken by multiple talkers rather than a single talker, while the manipulation of phonetic environment did not influence improvement.
